ONCORA-101 Trial: What You Need to Know Before You Participate

This summary explains the ONCORA-101 clinical trial in plain language. A clinical trial is a research study that tests whether a new medical treatment is safe and works. Read this carefully before deciding whether to join. If you have questions, ask the study doctor or nurse.

1. What is the purpose of this study?

The ONCORA-101 trial tests a new drug called BNV-ONC01. It is designed to treat advanced lung cancer that has spread and did not respond to prior treatment. This is a Phase 1 trial, which means this drug is being tested in people for the first time to see if it is safe and how your body responds to it. About 60 people will take part in this study.

2. What type of lung cancer do you need to have?

You can join this trial if you have non-small cell lung cancer, also called NSCLC. Your cancer must be advanced (stage IIIB or IV), which means it has spread beyond the original tumor. You must have already received at least one prior treatment for your cancer that did not fully work. A doctor must have confirmed your diagnosis with a tissue sample under a microscope.

3. What will happen during the study?

You will receive BNV-ONC01 as a treatment. The study uses "dose escalation," which means the dose starts low and gradually increases in small groups of participants. Your group may receive a higher dose than an earlier group, depending on how earlier participants respond.

You will visit the study clinic regularly for blood tests, imaging scans, and check-ins with the doctor. You will be monitored closely for any side effects or changes in your cancer. The exact number of visits depends on the study protocol (the detailed plan), but expect frequent appointments, especially at the start of treatment.

4. How long will you be in the study?

The length of your participation varies. You will receive the study drug for as long as it seems to help your cancer and you tolerate it without serious side effects. Even after you stop the drug, you may need follow-up visits to check on your health. The entire trial may last over a year, depending on how many participants join and how they respond.

5. What are the possible risks and side effects?

Because BNV-ONC01 is new, we do not know all the side effects yet. Side effects from similar cancer drugs can include fatigue, nausea, reduced blood cell counts, and infection. Some side effects may be serious or life-threatening. You could have an allergic reaction to the drug. There is a risk of serious complications that we cannot predict because this drug has never been given to people before. You will be monitored closely, and the study can stop or your dose can be lowered if serious problems occur.

6. What are the possible benefits?

The study drug may help shrink your tumor or stop it from growing. However, there is no guarantee this will happen. The main goal of Phase 1 trials is to test safety, not to prove that a drug works. Some participants may see benefit, but others may not.

7. Are there other treatment options?

Yes. Talk with your doctor about other cancer treatments available to you outside this trial, such as other chemotherapy drugs, targeted therapy, or clinical trials testing other new drugs.

8. How is your privacy protected?

Your medical information will be kept confidential and secured. Only study doctors and staff will see your information. Your identity will not be published in any reports about the study. However, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) may inspect study records to ensure safety.

9. Can you quit the study?

Yes. Joining this study is completely voluntary. You can stop at any time without penalty or loss of other care. Tell the study doctor if you want to leave.

10. Who do you contact with questions?

Ask your study doctor or nurse before you enroll and at any time during the trial. They are here to help you understand the risks and benefits.
clinical_consent_summary_oncora_phase3#a:
ONCORA-301 STUDY: What You Need to Know

This summary explains what you would agree to if you join the ONCORA-301 research study. Please read it carefully. A doctor will answer any questions you have before you decide whether to participate.

1. WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

The ONCORA-301 study tests a new medicine called a monoclonal antibody, or mAb. Think of it as a protein designed to help your immune system fight cancer. Researchers want to see if this medicine, when given along with standard lung cancer treatment, works better than standard treatment alone.

About 450 people with advanced lung cancer will join this study. BioNova Therapeutics is sponsoring the research.

2. WHAT TYPE OF LUNG CANCER QUALIFIES?

You must have non-small cell lung cancer, or NSCLC. Your cancer must be stage IIIB or stage IV, which means it is locally advanced or has spread. A biopsy or pathology report must confirm your diagnosis. You also must have cancer that can be measured on imaging scans like CT scans.

3. WHO CAN JOIN?

You can join if you:
- Are between 18 and 75 years old
- Have adequate heart, liver, and kidney function based on blood and imaging tests
- Have an ECOG score of 2 or lower. This score measures how well you can perform daily activities. A score of 0 means you feel well; a score of 2 means you spend more than half your day in bed or a chair but can still do some self-care.

4. WHO CANNOT JOIN?

You cannot join if you:
- Have an active autoimmune disease—a condition where your immune system mistakenly attacks your own body—such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus
- Have received anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy within the past 6 months. These are immune checkpoint inhibitors, medicines that work similarly to the study drug
- Have active cancer in your brain and spinal cord (called CNS metastases)
- Have had a heart attack, stroke, or severe heart condition within the past 6 months

5. WHAT WILL HAPPEN IF YOU JOIN?

You will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. Random assignment means a computer chooses your group, like flipping a coin. Neither you nor the doctor can choose which group you get.

Group 1 receives the new monoclonal antibody plus your standard cancer treatment.
Group 2 receives a placebo—a dummy injection with no active medicine—plus your standard cancer treatment.

You will not know which group you are in. This double-blind design helps researchers see if results come from the new medicine or from something else.

6. WHAT PROCEDURES ARE INVOLVED?

You will visit the clinic regularly for blood draws, imaging scans like CT scans, and physical exams. You will receive your assigned medicine by infusion, meaning it flows through an IV into your bloodstream. Visits may take several hours.

7. HOW LONG DOES THE STUDY LAST?

The study continues until the sponsor collects enough information to know if the medicine works. This may take months or longer. Your doctor will tell you how long your individual participation is expected to last.

8. WHAT ARE THE RISKS?

The new monoclonal antibody may cause side effects. Possible side effects include fatigue, nausea, rash, and immune-related reactions where your body's immune system becomes overactive. Serious but rare side effects could affect your lungs, liver, or heart. Blood tests and scans help doctors watch for problems.

9. WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS?

The medicine may help slow your cancer growth or shrink your tumor. However, this is a research study. We do not yet know if the new medicine will help you personally. You will still receive standard cancer treatment either way.

10. WHAT ARE OTHER TREATMENT OPTIONS?

Your doctor can explain other lung cancer treatments available outside this study, including chemotherapy, radiation, or other immunotherapies.

11. HOW IS YOUR INFORMATION PROTECTED?

Your medical information will be kept private and used only for this research. Your data will be stored securely and labeled with a code rather than your name.

12. CAN YOU CHANGE YOUR MIND?

Yes. Joining is voluntary. You can leave at any time without penalty or loss of medical care. Simply tell your doctor.

If you have questions, ask your study doctor before you decide.

My name is Sarah, and I'm living with HER2-positive breast cancer.

I first noticed something was wrong about a year ago. I felt a small lump in my left breast during my shower. At first, I tried to convince myself it was nothing serious, but deep down, I knew I needed to get it checked. That worry stayed with me for weeks before I finally called my doctor.

The diagnosis process was scary. I had imaging tests, and then a biopsy, which is when doctors take a tiny sample of tissue to look at under a microscope. I remember sitting in the waiting room, my hands shaking, trying to stay calm. When my doctor told me I had breast cancer and that my cancer was HER2-positive, I felt like the ground disappeared beneath me. HER2-positive means my cancer cells have extra copies of a protein called HER2, which makes the cancer grow faster.

Everything changed after that diagnosis. Some days I feel okay, and other days the exhaustion is overwhelming. Treatment days leave me tired and nauseous. I've lost my hair, which was harder emotionally than I expected. Simple things like grocery shopping or spending time with my kids take so much more effort now. I've had to say no to plans with friends, which sometimes makes me feel isolated.

But I've also discovered strength I didn't know I had. My family has rallied around me in ways that humble me. My ten-year-old daughter brings me tea when I'm not feeling well. My husband learned to cook my favorite meals. My friends check in constantly, even when I'm too tired to respond.

What gives me hope is my medical team. They believe in fighting this with me. I see other survivors in my support group who are living full lives years after their diagnosis. I see new treatments being developed specifically for HER2-positive cancer. Some days are really hard, but I hold onto the fact that people survive this. People thrive after this.

I'm taking it one day at a time. Some days that means celebrating small victories like having energy to take a walk or keeping food down. Other days it means just getting through. But I'm here, I'm fighting, and I'm not alone.

# Living with Type 2 Diabetes: My Story

My name is Marcus, and I've been living with Type 2 Diabetes for three years now. Looking back, I can see the warning signs were there all along, but I didn't know what I was looking at.

It started small. I'd feel exhausted after work, even if I'd sat at my desk most of the day. I was thirsty constantly, going through bottles of water like never before. I found myself making extra bathroom trips, which was annoying during meetings. I blamed it on stress and getting older. My wife finally said, "You need to get checked out," and I'm grateful she did.

My doctor ordered some blood tests. When the results came back, she explained that my body wasn't handling blood sugar the way it should. My pancreas, which makes a hormone called insulin, wasn't producing enough of it. Without enough insulin, sugar builds up in my bloodstream instead of getting into my cells for energy. She called it Type 2 Diabetes, and honestly, I felt scared and overwhelmed.

The first few months were an adjustment. I had to learn which foods affected my blood sugar and start checking my levels regularly. I couldn't just grab any snack I wanted anymore. Some days felt like too much work. My family had to change how we ate together, which wasn't easy for anyone.

But I've learned that having diabetes doesn't mean my life is over. It's different, yes. I think more about what I eat and when I exercise. I've developed routines that have become normal for me now. My doctor and I work together to manage my condition, and I've actually learned more about my body's health than I ever knew before.

What gives me hope is seeing how much better I feel when I take care of myself. My energy is back. The constant thirst is gone. I've met other people managing diabetes, and I see that many are living full, active lives. I want to be one of those people who looks back and knows they did everything they could to take care of their health.

It's not the diagnosis I wanted, but it's become part of my story.

# Learning to Live with My Type 2 Diabetes

My name is Marcus, and I've been living with Type 2 Diabetes for about five years now. Looking back, I realize the signs were there long before my diagnosis, but I didn't want to see them.

I remember feeling exhausted all the time. I'd wake up tired, drag through work, and crash by evening. I was constantly thirsty and kept making trips to the bathroom at night, which disrupted my sleep. I figured I was just getting older and stress was catching up with me. My wife finally convinced me to see my doctor when I noticed my vision getting blurry while reading.

The diagnosis hit hard. My doctor explained that my body wasn't using insulin properly. Insulin is a hormone that helps move sugar from your bloodstream into your cells for energy. With Type 2, my body either wasn't making enough or wasn't using it effectively, causing sugar to build up in my blood. The word "diabetes" felt like a life sentence, and honestly, I was scared.

The first year was the toughest. I had to completely rethink how I ate, exercise became non-negotiable, and monitoring my blood sugar became part of my routine. I felt frustrated missing certain foods and anxious about what this meant for my future. My wife had to learn along with me, supporting me while I adjusted.

But something shifted after those first months. I started noticing small wins. My energy improved. I could play with my grandkids without feeling completely drained. I discovered foods I actually enjoyed that worked with my new lifestyle. My doctor and I found a plan that felt manageable, not overwhelming.

What gives me hope is knowing I'm not alone. Millions of people manage Type 2 Diabetes every day. My numbers have improved, and I've gained control over my health in ways I didn't expect. Yes, this condition requires commitment and attention. But I've learned it doesn't define me.

If you've recently been diagnosed, I want you to know that the fear is normal, but so is learning to adapt. Take it one day at a time. Talk to your healthcare team. And be patient with yourself.

My name is Marcus, and I've been living with Type 2 Diabetes for five years now.

I didn't see it coming. I remember feeling tired all the time, even after sleeping nine hours. I'd get up to use the bathroom three or four times a night, which I figured was just part of getting older. Then I started getting these weird headaches and my vision felt a little blurry, especially toward the end of the day. I kept telling myself I needed new glasses.

One morning, I fainted at work. That scared me enough to finally go to the doctor.

The diagnosis was hard to hear. The doctor explained that my body wasn't using insulin the way it should—insulin is a hormone that helps control blood sugar, which is the glucose from the food we eat. My blood sugar was staying too high, and that's what Type 2 Diabetes means. I felt embarrassed, honestly. I thought diabetes only happened to people who didn't take care of themselves, but my doctor told me it's more complicated than that.

The first few months were rough. I had to change my eating habits, start checking my blood sugar regularly, and learn things I never thought I'd need to know. Some days felt overwhelming. I couldn't just grab whatever I wanted for lunch anymore. I had to think about everything differently.

What's helped most is realizing I'm not alone. I found a support group where other people understand exactly what I'm dealing with. They don't judge me on bad days, and they celebrate the wins with me.

Living with Type 2 Diabetes has changed my life, but it doesn't define me. Yes, I manage my condition every single day. Yes, it requires effort and planning. But I'm still me. I still do the things I love, spend time with my family, and work toward my goals.

What gives me hope is knowing that research is happening. New tools and treatments are being developed to help people like me. I take things one day at a time, and I've learned to be kinder to myself in the process.

My name is Marcus, and I was diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer, or NSCLC, eighteen months ago. I want to share my story with you.

I noticed something was wrong last spring. At first, I thought it was just a lingering cough from a cold. But weeks passed, and it wouldn't go away. I started feeling tired all the time, even after sleeping ten hours. Then I noticed I was losing weight without trying. I kept telling myself it was nothing serious, but deep down, I knew something wasn't right.

When I finally went to my doctor, they ordered some tests. I remember sitting in the imaging center, my heart pounding. A few days later, my doctor used the word I'll never forget: cancer. Specifically, they explained I had a tumor, which is an abnormal growth of cells, in my lung. Hearing those words felt like the ground disappeared beneath me. My wife held my hand while the doctor explained more about my condition and what came next. I felt scared, overwhelmed, and strangely numb all at once.

The diagnosis changed everything about my daily life. I went from working full-time to taking medical leave. Some days I'm too exhausted to do much more than sit on the couch. I've had to ask my family for help with things I used to do without thinking. Simple activities like climbing stairs or going grocery shopping now require planning and rest days. My wife became my caregiver, and that shift in our relationship took adjustment from both of us.

But I've also discovered unexpected sources of hope. My medical team has been incredible, walking me through each step. I've connected with other people facing similar battles, and their courage inspires me every single day. I've learned to appreciate small moments I used to take for granted, like my grandson's laugh or a sunny afternoon.

Living with NSCLC is hard. Some days are better than others. But I'm taking things one day at a time, leaning on my loved ones, and holding onto hope that tomorrow might bring something good. If you or someone you care about is facing this diagnosis, please know you're not alone in this journey.

# Living With Lung Cancer: My Story

My name is Marcus, and I'm learning to live with non-small cell lung cancer, or NSCLC. It's a type of lung tumor that started in my lungs and has changed everything about my life.

I first noticed something was wrong about eight months ago. I couldn't shake this persistent cough. At first, I figured it was just a cold that wouldn't go away. But after six weeks of coughing, especially in the mornings, I knew something wasn't right. I also felt more tired than usual, even after sleeping. My wife kept saying I sounded different when I talked. That's when I finally went to see my doctor.

The diagnosis hit hard. My doctor found a lung malignancy during imaging tests. Hearing those words felt like the floor dropped out from under me. I remember sitting in that office thinking about my daughter's wedding next year and wondering if I'd be there to walk her down the aisle.

My daily life looks completely different now. Some days the fatigue is overwhelming. I can't do yard work like I used to, and climbing stairs leaves me breathless. I've had to step back from my job as a construction supervisor, which was a huge part of my identity. My family has had to adjust too. My wife drives me to appointments, and my kids help more around the house.

But I've also found strength I didn't know I had. I've connected with other patients going through similar journeys. Hearing their stories reminds me I'm not alone in this. My medical team keeps working with me, and there are more options available now than ever before. I take things one day at a time instead of worrying about everything at once.

What gives me hope is my family's support and the dedicated people fighting to help patients like me. I think about my grandchildren and the moments still ahead of me. Some days are harder than others, but I'm choosing to focus on what I can do today rather than what I can't.

This journey is difficult, but I'm still here. I'm still fighting.

clinical_therapy_description_chemotherap:
UNDERSTANDING CHEMOTHERAPY TREATMENT

What Is Chemotherapy?

Chemotherapy is a type of cancer treatment that uses strong medicines to fight cancer cells. These medicines work throughout your whole body. Chemotherapy is sometimes used alone or combined with other treatments like surgery or radiation therapy.

How Does Chemotherapy Work?

Chemotherapy medicines attack cells that grow and divide quickly. Cancer cells grow faster than most normal cells, so these medicines target them. However, some healthy cells that also divide quickly can be affected too. This is why side effects happen.

Different chemotherapy drugs work in different ways. Some stop cancer cells from dividing. Others damage the cancer cell or trigger the cell to die. Your doctor will choose which medicine or combination of medicines is right for your specific cancer.

What to Expect During Treatment

Chemotherapy is usually given in cycles. You receive treatment for a period of time, then have a rest period to let your body recover. These cycles typically repeat for several months.

You may receive chemotherapy through a vein, as a pill, or through other methods depending on your treatment plan. Appointments may be at a hospital, cancer center, or outpatient clinic. Some treatments take a few minutes, while others take several hours.

Common Side Effects

Most side effects are temporary and manageable. Common ones include:

Nausea and vomiting. Many patients experience this, but anti-nausea medicines can help.

Hair loss. This happens because hair cells divide quickly, like cancer cells.

Fatigue. You may feel very tired during and after treatment.

Low blood cell counts. This can make you more likely to get infections, bruise easily, or feel short of breath.

Mouth sores. These can make eating and drinking uncomfortable.

Appetite changes. You may not feel like eating or may have a metallic taste in your mouth.

Other possible side effects include skin problems, nail changes, numbness or tingling in hands and feet, and diarrhea or constipation.

Side effects vary from person to person. Some people have mild side effects while others have more serious ones. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely and can help manage side effects when they happen.

Questions to Ask Your Doctor

Ask your doctor which specific chemotherapy drugs you will receive, how often you will have treatment, what side effects are most likely for you, and what you can do to manage side effects. Also ask about clinical trials that might be available to you.

Treatment is personal. Your healthcare team will work with you to create a plan that fits your needs and situation.
clinical_therapy_description_clinical-tr:
Understanding Clinical Trials: What You Should Know

What Is a Clinical Trial?

A clinical trial is a research study that tests whether a new treatment is safe and works well for patients. Before any new medicine or therapy can be approved for use, it must go through clinical trials. Trials help doctors and scientists understand if a treatment can help people with specific health conditions.

How Do Clinical Trials Work?

In a clinical trial, patients receive either the new treatment being tested or a standard treatment (or sometimes a placebo, which is a pill or injection with no active medicine). Researchers carefully watch how patients respond to see if the new treatment is safe and effective. Patients visit the trial site regularly for check-ups, blood tests, and other measurements.

BioNova Global Headquarters is currently running several clinical trials for different conditions:

ONCORA-301 and ONCORA-101 are testing treatments for non-small cell lung cancer. CARDIO-301 is studying a cardiovascular disease treatment. DIABPREV-201 is researching a type 2 diabetes therapy. HER2COMBO-201 is testing a treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer, a type of breast cancer with a specific protein. BREATHE-101 is examining a treatment for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, commonly called COPD, a serious lung disease. There is also a trial for hypertension, which is high blood pressure.

What to Expect During a Clinical Trial

If you join a trial, you will have an initial screening visit to make sure the trial is right for you. Then you will start receiving the study treatment. You will need to visit the trial site regularly, sometimes weekly or monthly, depending on the trial. At each visit, the research team will check your health, ask how you are feeling, and run tests.

Keeping a record of how you feel between visits helps the research team understand your experience. Be honest about any changes in your health or concerns.

Possible Side Effects

All treatments can cause side effects. Common side effects vary depending on the treatment but may include fatigue, nausea, headaches, or skin irritation. Some people experience no side effects, while others have more.

Your Participation Matters

Your decision to participate in a clinical trial is completely voluntary. You can ask questions at any time, and you can leave the trial whenever you want. Clinical trials help advance medical science and may help future patients. If you would like more information about any of these trials, speak with your doctor or visit the trial site directly.
clinical_therapy_description_clinical_tr:
CLINICAL TRIALS 101: TREATMENT OVERVIEW

What Is a Clinical Trial?

A clinical trial is a research study that tests whether a new medicine or treatment approach is safe and works for patients. BioNova Global Headquarters is running several clinical trials to help people with different health conditions. These trials follow strict rules to protect your safety and privacy.

How Clinical Trials Work

If you join a clinical trial, you receive either the new treatment being studied or a standard treatment (sometimes called a placebo—a pill or injection with no active medicine). Researchers track how the treatment affects you over time through regular doctor visits, blood tests, and other check-ins.

Current BioNova Trials

BioNova is studying treatments for:

Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (ONCORA-301, ONCORA-101) — a common type of lung cancer
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (DIABPREV-201) — when your body has trouble controlling blood sugar
Cardiovascular Disease (CARDIO-301) — conditions affecting your heart and blood vessels
HER2-Positive Breast Cancer (HER2COMBO-201) — a specific type of breast cancer
Hypertension (high blood pressure)
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease or COPD (BREATHE-101) — long-term lung disease that makes breathing difficult

What to Expect During Treatment

Treatment schedules vary depending on which trial you join. You might receive pills, injections, or infusions at a clinic. Visits may happen weekly, monthly, or less often. Before starting, researchers explain everything and answer your questions.

Common Side Effects

Most treatments can cause side effects—unwanted changes your body experiences. Common ones include fatigue, nausea, headache, or skin reactions. Not everyone experiences the same side effects, and some may be mild while others are more serious. Your research team monitors you closely and can help manage side effects.

Your Rights as a Participant

You can ask questions anytime. You can leave the trial whenever you want, for any reason, without penalty. All information about you stays confidential. Your medical care continues whether you stay in the trial or not.

Getting Started

If you're interested in learning whether a trial might be right for you, talk with your doctor. They can help determine if you meet the study requirements. BioNova staff will provide detailed information about what participation involves, including any risks.

Remember: Joining a clinical trial is always your choice. Take time to understand what's involved before deciding.
clinical_therapy_description_immunothera:
Understanding Immunotherapy: An Overview for Patients and Caregivers

What Is Immunotherapy?

Immunotherapy is a type of cancer treatment that helps your body's own immune system fight cancer cells. Your immune system is made up of cells and proteins that protect you from infections and diseases. Sometimes cancer cells can hide from your immune system, making it hard for your body to find and destroy them. Immunotherapy works by helping your immune system recognize and attack these hidden cancer cells.

How Does Immunotherapy Work?

Think of your immune system like your body's security team. Cancer cells sometimes wear a "disguise" that tricks your security team into ignoring them. Immunotherapy removes this disguise or gives your immune system better tools to recognize the danger. This helps your body's natural defenses work harder to find and destroy cancer cells.

What to Expect During Treatment

Immunotherapy is usually given through an IV, which is a small tube placed in your vein. Treatment sessions happen at regular intervals that your doctor will explain. Each session typically takes a few hours. Most people continue treatment over several months. Your doctor will schedule regular appointments to check how you are responding to treatment.

Common Side Effects

Like all medical treatments, immunotherapy can cause side effects. These vary from person to person and can include:

Fatigue, which means feeling very tired
Skin reactions like rashes or itching
Nausea or loss of appetite
Fever or chills
Headaches
Joint or muscle pain
Shortness of breath or cough
Diarrhea

Some side effects happen during treatment sessions, while others may develop days or weeks later. Most side effects are manageable, but some can be serious. Tell your doctor right away if you have any new symptoms or if existing symptoms get worse.

Clinical Trials at BioNova Global Headquarters

BioNova Global Headquarters is studying immunotherapy for several conditions through clinical trials. These trials help us understand how well immunotherapy works and how to make treatments safer. If you have questions about whether a clinical trial might be right for you, talk with your doctor.

Important Reminders

Immunotherapy is not right for everyone. Your doctor will decide if this treatment makes sense based on your specific condition and health history. Always discuss benefits, risks, and what to expect with your healthcare team before starting any new treatment. Your questions and concerns matter.
clinical_therapy_description_mab-therapy:
Understanding MAb Therapy: What You Need to Know

What Is MAb Therapy?

MAb stands for monoclonal antibody. It is a type of medicine made in a laboratory to help your immune system fight disease. Think of antibodies as your body's natural defense workers. MAb therapy uses specially designed antibodies that target specific parts of diseased cells or proteins in your body.

How Does MAb Therapy Work?

Your immune system normally creates antibodies to recognize and fight harmful invaders like germs. MAb therapy works by creating antibodies in the lab that are trained to find and attach to specific targets in your body. Once attached, these antibodies can block harmful proteins, slow disease growth, or help your immune system attack problem cells. Different MAb therapies target different diseases, so each medicine works in its own way.

What to Expect During Treatment

MAb therapy is usually given through an IV, which means the medicine goes directly into your bloodstream through a needle in your vein. Some treatments may be given as an injection under your skin. Your healthcare team will schedule regular appointments for you to receive your doses. You may need to come in weekly, monthly, or on another schedule depending on your specific medicine.

Before and after each treatment, your healthcare team will monitor you closely. They will check your vital signs, run blood tests, and ask how you are feeling. These visits help your doctor make sure the treatment is working and that you are handling it well.

Common Side Effects

Like all medicines, MAb therapy can cause side effects. The most common ones include:

Flu-like symptoms such as fever, chills, and body aches
Tiredness and weakness
Headaches
Nausea or vomiting
Diarrhea or constipation
Skin rashes or itching
Pain or redness at the injection or IV site
High blood pressure
Shortness of breath

Side effects can happen during treatment or in the days after. Many side effects get better on their own or can be managed with other medicines. Some side effects are serious and need immediate medical attention, such as difficulty breathing, chest pain, or severe allergic reactions.

What BioNova Global Is Studying

BioNova Global Headquarters is researching MAb therapy for several conditions including certain types of lung cancer, breast cancer, heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, and lung disease. We are conducting clinical trials like ONCORA-301, ONCORA-101, CARDIO-301, DIABPREV-201, HER2COMBO-201, and BREATHE-101 to learn more about how these treatments work and how safe they are.

Talk with your healthcare team about whether MAb therapy might be right for you and what to expect.
clinical_therapy_description_mab_therapy:
Understanding Monoclonal Antibody Therapy

Monoclonal antibody therapy, often called mab therapy, is a type of medicine that works with your immune system to help treat certain conditions. BioNova Global Headquarters is researching this approach for several health conditions, including certain cancers, heart disease, diabetes, lung disease, and high blood pressure.

What Is Monoclonal Antibody Therapy?

Monoclonal antibodies are proteins made in a laboratory that are designed to find and attach to specific targets in your body. Think of them like specially trained search-and-rescue workers that can identify problem areas and either mark them for your immune system to destroy or block harmful signals.

How It Works

Your immune system naturally produces antibodies to fight infection and disease. Scientists can now create antibodies in the lab that target cancer cells, inflammatory proteins, or other disease-causing substances. Once these antibodies are in your body, they travel through your bloodstream looking for their specific target. When they find it, they attach and either kill the harmful cells directly or signal your immune system to do the job.

What to Expect During Treatment

Monoclonal antibody therapy is typically given as an infusion, meaning the medicine is delivered through an IV line into a vein, usually in your arm. A single infusion can take 30 minutes to several hours depending on the specific treatment. You may receive infusions once a week, once a month, or at different intervals depending on your condition and treatment plan.

Before starting treatment, your healthcare team will do blood tests and other evaluations to make sure this therapy is right for you. They will also discuss what to expect and answer your questions.

Common Side Effects

Like all medicines, monoclonal antibodies can cause side effects. The most common are flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, fatigue, and muscle aches. These usually happen during or shortly after the infusion and often improve with time.

Other possible side effects may include infusion reactions (symptoms like rash, difficulty breathing, or chest discomfort that occur during treatment), low blood counts, nausea, or headache.

More serious side effects are possible but less common. Your healthcare team will monitor you carefully during and after infusions to watch for any problems.

Your Treatment Team

Throughout your treatment, you will work closely with doctors, nurses, and other healthcare professionals who specialize in mab therapy. They will track how you respond to treatment and manage any side effects that develop. Regular blood tests and imaging may be needed to see how well the treatment is working.

If you have questions about whether monoclonal antibody therapy might be appropriate for your condition, talk with your healthcare provider about what could be right for you.
clinical_therapy_description_radiation#1:
RADIATION TREATMENT: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

Radiation therapy uses high-energy beams of light to target and destroy cancer cells. It is one way doctors treat certain types of cancer, including non-small cell lung cancer and HER2-positive breast cancer.

HOW RADIATION THERAPY WORKS

Radiation damages the DNA inside cancer cells, which stops them from growing and dividing. Healthy cells in the treatment area may also be affected, but they often repair themselves better than cancer cells do. Your doctor will plan your treatment carefully to aim radiation at the cancer while protecting as much healthy tissue as possible.

WHAT TO EXPECT DURING TREATMENT

Before your first treatment, you will have a planning session. During this visit, your doctor will use imaging scans to map out exactly where the radiation will go. This helps make sure the radiation hits the right spot.

During each radiation session, you will lie still on a table. A machine called a linear accelerator will move around you and deliver radiation from different angles. Each session usually takes 15 to 30 minutes. You will not feel pain during the treatment itself, though you may hear buzzing or clicking sounds.

Most people receive radiation several days a week for several weeks. Your doctor will tell you how many treatments you need.

COMMON SIDE EFFECTS

Side effects depend on where the radiation is aimed and how much treatment you receive. They may include:

Skin changes in the treated area, like redness, dryness, or peeling

Fatigue, or feeling very tired

Nausea or loss of appetite

Hair loss in the treated area

Difficulty swallowing if radiation targets your chest or throat

Cough or shortness of breath if radiation targets your lungs or chest

Most side effects improve after treatment ends, though some may last longer. Your doctor and care team can suggest ways to manage these effects and feel more comfortable.

STAYING INFORMED

Talk with your doctor about what to expect based on your specific situation. Ask about any clinical trials that might be right for you, such as those offered through BioNova Global Headquarters. Your medical team is here to answer your questions and support you throughout your treatment.

Remember, radiation therapy affects each person differently. Keep in close contact with your healthcare team so they can monitor how you are doing and adjust your care plan if needed.
clinical_therapy_description_targeted-th:
Understanding Targeted Therapy

What Is Targeted Therapy?

Targeted therapy is a type of medicine that works by finding and attacking specific parts of cancer cells or disease cells that help them grow and survive. Unlike some other treatments, targeted therapy aims to affect mainly the cells causing disease while limiting damage to healthy cells. This approach is used to treat certain types of cancer and other serious health conditions.

How Targeted Therapy Works

Every cell in your body has different characteristics. Some disease cells have special features or mutations, which are changes in their genetic material, that make them different from healthy cells. Targeted therapy medicines are designed to recognize these specific features and block them. Think of it like a key fitting into a lock. The medicine targets the exact "lock" that is causing the problem.

For example, some breast cancer cells have extra copies of a protein called HER2. Targeted therapy can work by blocking this protein so the cancer cells cannot grow. In lung cancer, certain cells may have mutations that help them survive. Targeted therapy can stop these specific mutations from working.

What to Expect During Treatment

Your doctor will test your cells to see if you are a good candidate for targeted therapy. This helps make sure the medicine will work for your specific condition. If targeted therapy is right for you, you will likely take it as a pill by mouth or receive it as an injection or infusion, which means medicine given through a needle into your vein.

Treatment schedules vary. You may take medicine daily, weekly, or on another schedule. You will have regular appointments to check how you are doing and whether the treatment is working.

Common Side Effects

Targeted therapy side effects vary depending on the specific medicine. Common side effects may include:

- Skin problems like rashes or dryness
- Diarrhea or other digestive issues
- Fatigue, meaning extreme tiredness
- Nausea
- Heart problems in some cases
- Liver changes that your doctor will monitor with blood tests

Most side effects are manageable, but some can be serious. Tell your doctor right away if you have new or worsening symptoms.

Working With Your Healthcare Team

Targeted therapy works best when you follow your treatment plan closely. Keep all appointments, take medicines exactly as prescribed, and report any side effects immediately. Your doctor and care team can help manage side effects and adjust your treatment if needed.

If you have questions about whether targeted therapy might be right for you, talk with your healthcare provider. BioNova Global Headquarters supports patients and caregivers throughout their treatment journey.
clinical_therapy_description_targeted_th:
UNDERSTANDING TARGETED THERAPY: A PATIENT GUIDE

What Is Targeted Therapy?

Targeted therapy is a type of treatment that works differently than traditional medicines. Instead of affecting your whole body, targeted therapies are designed to attack specific parts of disease cells or the conditions causing your illness. Think of it like using a lock-and-key system—the medication is made to fit and affect only certain targets in your body.

How Does Targeted Therapy Work?

Your doctor will first test your condition to identify specific characteristics or markers that make you a good candidate for targeted therapy. For example, some cancer cells have specific proteins on their surface, some people with diabetes have particular genetic factors, and some heart or lung conditions involve specific pathways in the body.

Once your doctor understands your individual situation, they can prescribe a targeted therapy designed to work with your specific condition. The medication blocks or changes how disease cells or disease processes function, which may help slow or stop the problem.

What Can You Expect During Treatment?

Targeted therapy is usually taken as a pill, injection, or infusion (medicine given through an IV line into your vein). Your treatment schedule depends on your condition and the specific medication. Some people take medication daily, while others may have treatments scheduled weekly or monthly. Your medical team will explain your exact schedule and what to expect at each appointment.

Regular visits with your doctor are important. You'll have blood tests and other check-ups to see how the treatment is working and watch for any changes in your health.

Common Side Effects

Side effects vary depending on the type of targeted therapy and your individual health. Possible effects may include:

Fatigue (feeling very tired)
Nausea or loss of appetite
Rash or skin changes
Diarrhea or constipation
Headaches
Joint or muscle pain

Most side effects are manageable, and your medical team can suggest ways to help. Tell your doctor about any side effects you experience—they may be able to adjust your dose or recommend additional support.

Important Things to Know

Targeted therapy works best when you take it exactly as prescribed. Missing doses can reduce how well it works. Let your doctor know about all other medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, because some may interact with your treatment.

If you're enrolled in a clinical trial, such as ONCORA-301, CARDIO-301, or BREATHE-101, your medical team will provide additional information specific to that study.

Talk with your healthcare team about what to expect for your individual situation. They can answer your specific questions and help you prepare for treatment.
clinical_trial_faq_cardio-outcomes#c25b1:
CARDIO-301 Trial: Frequently Asked Questions

What is the CARDIO-301 trial?

The CARDIO-301 trial is a research study that tests whether a new medicine called BNV-CRD01 can help people with heart disease. BioNova Therapeutics is sponsoring this study to see if this medicine is safe and works better than a placebo (a fake pill with no medicine in it).

Who can join the CARDIO-301 trial?

You can join if you are between 40 and 80 years old and have been diagnosed with coronary artery disease, which is a narrowing of the blood vessels that supply your heart. You also need to have high blood pressure (above 140 mmHg) and high cholesterol levels, even while taking medicines to control them. Your doctor will check your overall health and kidney function to make sure it is safe for you to participate.

Who cannot join this trial?

You cannot join if you have very severe heart failure, have had a recent stroke, or have serious kidney problems. You also cannot participate if you have uncontrolled atrial fibrillation, which is a condition where your heart beats irregularly, or if you are planning to have a heart procedure in the next three months.

What will happen if I join the trial?

If you join, you will receive either one of two doses of BNV-CRD01 or a placebo, and you will be assigned to one of these groups randomly, like flipping a coin. You will take your assigned medicine while continuing your regular heart medicines and visiting the study center for check-ups and blood tests.

How long will I be in the study?

The exact length of the study will be explained to you by the research team, but you will need to commit to regular visits for monitoring and blood work. Make sure to ask the study team about the full timeline before you decide to join.

Will I know which medicine I am taking?

No, the study is designed so that neither you nor the study team will know whether you are taking BNV-CRD01 or a placebo. This helps ensure the results are fair and not influenced by what you or your doctor expect to happen.

What are the possible side effects?

Like all medicines, BNV-CRD01 may cause side effects, though we do not yet know all of them since this is a research study testing a new medicine. The study team will monitor you closely and will tell you about any side effects that are found. You should report any unusual symptoms to the study team right away.

Will the trial cost me money?

The study sponsor covers the cost of the study medicine and study-related medical tests and visits. You should ask the study team about what costs, if any, you might need to pay, such as travel expenses to the study center.

Can I stop the trial whenever I want?

Yes, you can leave the study at any time and for any reason, without penalty. If you decide to stop, you can continue taking your regular heart medicines as prescribed by your regular doctor.

What if I am harmed during the trial?

BioNova Therapeutics has insurance to cover injuries that occur because of study participation. If you experience a serious problem, tell the study team immediately so you can receive proper care and the injury can be documented.

How many people are enrolled in this trial?

So far, 342 people out of a planned 600 have enrolled in the CARDIO-301 trial. The study team is still recruiting more participants.

How do I sign up for CARDIO-301?

Talk to your cardiologist or your primary care doctor about whether this trial might be right for you. Your doctor can help you contact the study team, or you can ask for the study contact information at your hospital or clinic.
clinical_trial_faq_cardio_outcomes#5f1f5:
CARDIO-301 TRIAL: FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

What is the CARDIO-301 trial?

CARDIO-301 is a research study testing a new medication called BNV-CRD01 to help people with heart disease. BioNova Therapeutics is running this study to see if this medicine can help reduce heart problems in people ages 40 to 80. The study is currently enrolling participants and is in Phase 3, which is the final stage before the FDA reviews the medication.

Who can join this study?

You may be eligible if you are between 40 and 80 years old and have been diagnosed with coronary artery disease (narrowing of the blood vessels that supply your heart). You also need to have a systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg (the top number in your blood pressure reading) even while taking blood pressure medications, and your LDL cholesterol (the "bad" cholesterol) must be above 70 mg/dL. Your doctor can tell you if your medical history and current health meet all the requirements.

Who should not join this study?

You would not be eligible if you have severe heart failure (a condition where your heart cannot pump enough blood), have had a recent stroke, have severely reduced kidney function, or have uncontrolled atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat that your current medicines do not manage well). Additionally, if you are planning to have a coronary intervention (a procedure to open blocked arteries) within the next three months, you cannot participate. Your study doctor will review your complete medical history to confirm whether the study is safe for you.

What does participation involve?

Participants will receive either a 10 mg dose of BNV-CRD01, a 25 mg dose of BNV-CRD01, or a placebo (a pill with no active medication), assigned randomly. You will have regular clinic visits for blood tests, blood pressure checks, and heart monitoring. The study team will track your health throughout the trial to watch for any changes or side effects.

How often do I need to visit the clinic?

The exact schedule of visits will be explained to you by the study team, but you should expect regular appointments throughout the trial period. Visits typically include blood work and heart-related evaluations to monitor your health. The study team will work with you to schedule visits at convenient times.

What are the possible risks of joining?

Like all medications, BNV-CRD01 may cause side effects, though we do not yet know all of them since this medicine is still being tested. Common side effects from similar heart medicines can include headache, dizziness, or stomach upset, though not everyone experiences these. The study team will monitor you closely and will stop your participation immediately if they see any serious safety concerns.

What are the potential benefits?

BNV-CRD01 is being tested because early research suggests it may help reduce the risk of heart problems in people with coronary artery disease. However, there is no guarantee that this medicine will help you personally, since the study is still determining if it works. Some participants may receive a placebo instead of the active medication.

Will the study cost me money?

The study sponsor covers the cost of the study drug and most study-related visits and tests. You may have out-of-pocket costs related to your regular medical care that are not directly part of the study, so you should ask the study team about what costs you might be responsible for. Travel expenses to clinic visits are typically your responsibility unless the study team discusses other arrangements with you.

What happens if I experience a serious side effect?

The study team monitors all participants closely for safety, and they have trained staff and emergency procedures in place to help you immediately. You should report any concerning symptoms to the study team right away, and you can withdraw from the study at any time without penalty. The study includes insurance and medical care coverage for study-related injuries.

How long is the study?

The exact duration will be provided by the study team during enrollment, but Phase 3 trials typically last several months to over a year depending on the research questions being answered. You will be told the expected time commitment before you decide to participate. The study team will keep you informed about the timeline throughout your involvement.

Can I continue my regular heart medications?

Yes, you will continue taking your regular blood pressure and heart medications during the study. The study drug (BNV-CRD01 or placebo) is added to your existing treatment plan, not as a replacement. Your study doctor will review all your current medications to make sure they work safely with the study drug.

How do I enroll in CARDIO-301?

Talk to your primary care doctor or cardiologist about the study, or you can visit BioNova Therapeutics' website or call their patient enrollment line to learn more about locations near you. A study team member will review your medical records and discuss whether you meet the eligibility requirements. If you are a good fit, you will have an in-person screening visit to confirm your eligibility before you officially join.

Can I withdraw from the study at any time?

Yes, you can withdraw from the study at any time without any penalty and without affecting your regular medical care. If you decide to leave, simply let the study team know, and they will make sure your transition back to your regular doctors is smooth. Your decision to participate is entirely voluntary.
clinical_trial_faq_copd-inhaler#9e0826fe:
BREATHE-101 Clinical Trial: Frequently Asked Questions

ABOUT THE TRIAL

What is the BREATHE-101 trial studying?

BREATHE-101 is a research study testing a new medicine called BNV-CPD01 to see if it can help people with COPD, a lung disease that makes it hard to breathe. The study will compare two different doses of this medicine against a placebo, which is a fake medicine that looks real but has no active ingredient, to find out if the medicine is safe and if it works.

Who is BioNova Therapeutics?

BioNova Therapeutics is the company that created BNV-CPD01 and is running this research study. They work with doctors and hospitals to test new treatments for people with serious lung diseases.

ELIGIBILITY AND PARTICIPATION

Am I eligible to join this trial?

You may be eligible if you are between 40 and 80 years old, have been diagnosed with COPD, have had at least one flare-up of your COPD symptoms in the past year, and have a smoking history of at least 10 pack-years (for example, smoking one pack a day for 10 years). Your lung function also needs to be in a certain range, and your overall health needs to be stable enough for the study.

What does "pack-year history" mean?

A pack-year is a way to measure how much someone has smoked over time. One pack-year means smoking one pack of cigarettes per day for one full year. If you smoked half a pack per day for 20 years, that would be 10 pack-years.

What conditions would prevent me from joining?

You cannot join if you currently have asthma, have been diagnosed with lung cancer, use more than 4 liters of supplemental oxygen per minute, have had an active respiratory infection in the past 4 weeks, or have had lung transplant or lung volume reduction surgery in the past. If you have any of these conditions, please discuss with your doctor whether this study is right for you.

WHAT TO EXPECT

What will happen during the trial?

If you join the study, you will be randomly assigned to receive either a low dose of BNV-CPD01, a high dose of BNV-CPD01, or a placebo. You will not know which treatment you are receiving. You will have visits with the study team where they will check your lungs, ask about your symptoms, and monitor your health throughout the study.

How long will I be in the trial?

This is a Phase 1 trial, which is the earliest stage of testing a new medicine in people. Phase 1 trials are typically shorter than later-stage studies, but the exact length of BREATHE-101 will be explained to you in detail before you decide to join. Your study coordinator will provide you with a complete timeline.

What are the time commitments involved?

You will need to come to clinic visits at set times during the study, and these visits may include breathing tests, blood draws, and talking with doctors about how you are feeling. Your study coordinator will give you a schedule of all required visits so you can plan ahead and make sure you can commit to the study.

COSTS, RISKS, AND BENEFITS

Will I have to pay to be in this trial?

No. There is no cost to you to participate in this clinical trial. All study-related medical care and tests are provided at no charge, though you may need to cover your own transportation to visits.

What are the risks of participating?

Like all medicines, BNV-CPD01 may cause side effects, though we do not yet know what these might be since this is the first time the medicine is being tested in people. The breathing tests and blood draws required for the study are generally safe but can cause minor discomfort. If you have any serious health problems during the study, the research team will monitor you closely and can stop your participation if needed to keep you safe.

What are the possible benefits?

Some people in the trial may feel better or have fewer breathing problems if BNV-CPD01 works well. However, you might receive the placebo, in which case you would not receive the active medicine. Even if BNV-CPD01 does not help you directly, the information learned from your participation will help researchers develop better treatments for people with COPD in the future.

ENROLLMENT

How do I enroll, and when can I start?

The trial is not yet recruiting, which means we are still preparing to open enrollment. BioNova Therapeutics will announce when the trial is ready to accept participants. You can contact your doctor or reach out to BioNova Global Headquarters for more information about how to express your interest and be notified when enrollment begins.
clinical_trial_faq_copd_inhaler#52dea806:
BREATHE-101 Trial: Frequently Asked Questions

What is the BREATHE-101 trial?

BREATHE-101 is a research study testing a new medication called BNV-CPD01 to help people with COPD, a lung disease that makes breathing difficult. This is an early-stage study (called Phase 1) where we are primarily checking if the medication is safe and well-tolerated.

Who can participate in this trial?

You may be eligible if you are between 40 and 80 years old, have been diagnosed with COPD, have had at least one flare-up (called an exacerbation) of your symptoms in the past year, and have a significant smoking history of at least 10 pack-years (meaning 10 cigarettes a day for 10 years, or equivalent). We will also check your lung function to make sure it falls within the study range.

Who cannot participate in this trial?

You would not be eligible if you have active asthma, lung cancer, or a respiratory infection within the past 4 weeks. You also cannot participate if you use supplemental oxygen above 4 liters per minute, or if you have had a lung transplant or lung volume reduction surgery in the past.

What does the study involve?

The study will involve visits to our research clinic where you will receive either a low dose of BNV-CPD01, a high dose of BNV-CPD01, or a placebo (inactive treatment that looks like the real medication but has no active ingredient). We will monitor your health closely with breathing tests, blood work, and other assessments.

How long will I be in the study?

The exact duration will be discussed with the research team once you enroll, but Phase 1 trials typically involve several weeks to a few months of active participation plus follow-up visits. We will provide you with a detailed schedule during the informed consent discussion.

What is a placebo and why is it used?

A placebo is a treatment that looks identical to the real medication but contains no active ingredient. Placebos help us understand what improvement happens naturally versus what happens because of the actual medication. About one-third of study participants will receive a placebo.

Will the study cost me anything?

Study visits and all trial-related medical care and testing will be provided at no cost to you. We will also discuss compensation for your time and travel expenses. Please ask the research team about specific details regarding payment.

What are the possible risks of participating?

Like all medications, BNV-CPD01 may cause side effects, though we do not yet know what these might be since this is an early-stage study. Possible risks include mild to moderate reactions at the injection or application site, temporary changes in how you feel, or other effects we will monitor closely. The research team will explain all known risks before you decide whether to join.

What are the possible benefits?

We hope that BNV-CPD01 may help improve your breathing and reduce COPD flare-ups, though we cannot guarantee this in a Phase 1 study. Even if you do not experience direct medical benefit, your participation will help us develop better treatments for people with COPD.

How is my safety monitored during the trial?

Your safety is our top priority. We will perform regular breathing tests, blood work, and check your vital signs at each visit. You will have direct contact with the research team, and you can call us anytime if you have concerns or experience new symptoms between visits.

Can I stop participating if I change my mind?

Yes, you can withdraw from the study at any time without penalty and without affecting your regular medical care. If you decide to leave, we will discuss any necessary follow-up care to keep you safe.

How do I enroll or learn more?

To express interest or ask more questions, please contact BioNova Therapeutics directly through our website or call our patient recruitment team. A member of our research staff will discuss eligibility, answer your questions, and guide you through the enrollment process if you choose to participate.
clinical_trial_faq_diabetes-prevention#b:
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ABOUT THE DIABPREV-201 STUDY

What is the DIABPREV-201 study?

The DIABPREV-201 study is a research trial testing a new medication called BNV-DX01 to see if it can help people with type 2 diabetes manage their blood sugar better. BioNova Therapeutics is sponsoring this study to understand whether this medicine is safe and effective. We're currently enrolling participants and have nearly completed our target of 300 people.

Who can join the DIABPREV-201 study?

You can join if you are between 30 and 70 years old, have type 2 diabetes, and have been taking a stable dose of metformin (a diabetes medicine) for at least 3 months. You also need to have a BMI between 25 and 40 and a blood sugar level (HbA1c) between 7.0% and 10.5%. Your kidney function also needs to be at a certain level, which we'll check with a simple blood test.

Who cannot participate in this study?

You cannot join if you have type 1 diabetes or gestational diabetes, or if your kidneys are not working well enough. You also cannot participate if you have had diabetic ketoacidosis in the past, if you have taken insulin in the last 3 months, or if you are unable to have an ECOG score of 1 or better, which means you should be able to do light activities. Your study team can explain what this means for your specific situation.

What will happen if I join the study?

If you decide to participate, you will receive either the new medicine BNV-DX01 at a low dose, BNV-DX01 at a higher dose, or a placebo (a pill with no active medicine). You won't know which one you're getting because the study is blinded, meaning the research team also won't know which treatment you have. You'll have regular visits to the clinic where we'll check your blood sugar, take blood tests, and ask how you're feeling.

Will I have to stop taking my current diabetes medicines?

No, you will continue taking your metformin at the same dose you have been taking. The study medicine or placebo is being tested in addition to your metformin, not instead of it. If you are taking other diabetes medicines besides metformin, talk with your study doctor about whether they need to be adjusted.

How much time will the study take?

The exact time commitment will be explained during your screening visit, but you should expect regular clinic visits spaced throughout the study period. Each visit may take a couple of hours, including time for check-in, blood tests, and talking with the study team. Your study doctor will give you a detailed schedule so you can plan ahead.

Will it cost me money to participate?

Study visits and procedures related to the research are provided free of charge to you. However, you should ask your study team about parking, transportation, and other practical details when you call to learn more. Your regular health insurance may still apply to any medical care outside of the study visits.

What are the possible risks of joining this study?

Like any medicine, BNV-DX01 may cause side effects, though we don't yet know all of them because this is an early-stage study. Common side effects from similar medicines can include headache, nausea, or dizziness. There is also a chance you could receive a placebo and not get the active medicine, which means your diabetes care might not improve during the study.

What if I experience a bad side effect during the study?

Your safety is our top priority, and our research team is trained to handle any health concerns that come up. You should tell your study doctor right away about any new or troubling symptoms, and you can always call the study center if you have questions between visits. You have the right to stop participating in the study at any time if you feel it is not right for you.

Can I stop taking the study medicine whenever I want?

Yes, you can withdraw from the study at any time without giving a reason, and there will be no penalty or loss of benefits. If you decide to leave, we'll make sure your regular diabetes care continues smoothly and that your personal doctor knows about any changes. We'll also discuss the safest way to stop the study medicine if you've been taking the active treatment.

How will I find out if the study medicine actually works?

The main results of this study will be shared with the medical community, and your study team will tell you about the findings once the research is complete. If you received the active medicine, your blood sugar levels during the study will give you and your doctor useful information about how it worked for you personally. You may also learn important information that helps guide your diabetes care moving forward.

How do I sign up for DIABPREV-201?

To express interest or learn more, you can contact BioNova Global Headquarters or ask your regular diabetes doctor if they know about enrollment sites near you. During your first visit, a member of the study team will explain everything in detail and answer all your questions before you decide to participate. There is no obligation to join, and you can take time to think it over and discuss it with your family and doctor.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ABOUT DIABPREV-201

What is the DIABPREV-201 study?

DIABPREV-201 is a research study testing whether a new medicine called BNV-DX01 can help people with type 2 diabetes manage their condition better. This is a phase 2 study, which means we are still learning if the medicine is safe and works the way we hope it will.

Who can join this study?

You may be able to join if you are between 30 and 70 years old, have type 2 diabetes, are generally in good health, and have been taking a stable dose of metformin for at least three months. Your diabetes control level (measured by a blood test called HbA1c) should be between 7.0% and 10.5%, and your weight should fall within certain ranges for your height.

What medical conditions would keep me from joining?

You cannot join if you have type 1 diabetes or gestational diabetes, or if you have had severe kidney problems (eGFR below 45). You also cannot participate if you have a history of diabetic ketoacidosis, which is a serious diabetes emergency, or if you have used insulin within the past three months.

What does the study involve?

You will receive either the test medicine BNV-DX01 at one of two doses, or a placebo (a pill with no medicine), and we will track how it affects your diabetes over time. You will have regular visits to the study center for blood tests, blood pressure checks, and other routine health measurements.

How long will I be in the study?

The exact length depends on the study design, but you should expect multiple visits over several months. We will tell you the full schedule before you decide to join so you can plan accordingly.

What is the time commitment for each visit?

Most visits take between one and two hours, including time for check-in, talking with the study team, blood work, and other health measurements. Some visits may be shorter and some longer, depending on what tests are being done that day.

Will the study cost me money?

There is no cost to you for the study medicine or the medical visits required by the research. However, you may need to cover your own travel to the study center unless otherwise arranged.

What are the possible risks?

Like all medicines, BNV-DX01 may cause side effects, though we do not yet know how common they are or how serious they might be. We will monitor you closely throughout the study and tell you right away if we find any safety concerns.

How will my privacy be protected?

All information you share will be kept private and secure, and your personal identity will not be used in any study reports or publications. Only the study team and authorized people will have access to your medical information.

How do I enroll or get more information?

You can contact BioNova Global Headquarters through your healthcare provider, or ask about the study at your diabetes clinic. The study team will answer your questions and help you decide if DIABPREV-201 is right for you.

Can I stop participating whenever I want?

Yes, you can leave the study at any time for any reason, and doing so will not affect your regular medical care. We just ask that you let the study team know so they can follow up on your health.

What happens after the study ends?

The study team will discuss the results with you and explain what they mean for your diabetes care. Depending on the findings, your regular doctor may talk with you about next steps for your treatment.
